My Approach

Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP, brings nearly 10 years of counseling experience and provides trauma informed, trauma focused care for adults and couples in person in North Fort Worth and virtually throughout Texas.

Her work focuses on trauma, PTSD, complex trauma, anxiety, ADHD, depression, emotional dysregulation, relationship concerns, boundaries, and major life transitions. She has extensive experience working with first responders, military veterans, and their families, including the cumulative stress, identity demands, and relationship challenges connected to service oriented careers.

Stacy uses evidence based assessment and treatment planning to develop an individualized approach based on each client’s symptoms, history, goals, and lived experience. Her style is down to earth, nonjudgmental, culturally responsive, and focused on helping clients build insight, strengthen relationships, establish healthier boundaries, process trauma, and improve emotional resilience.

Additional Professional Work

In addition to counseling, Stacy provides clinical supervision for LPC Associates and master’s-level counseling students. She also offers consultation, professional training, and wellness programming related to trauma, law enforcement mental health, ADHD, resilience, and the mental health needs of first responders, military veterans, and their families.

Stacy has developed Steel Armor Mindset, a trauma-informed, culturally competent program created for first responders, command staff, administrative personnel and veterans. The curriculum teaches regulation, identity repair, emotional stability, and long-term resilience without pathologizing survival or minimizing institutional realities.

/frequently-asked-questions/.title: Frequently Asked Questions
/frequently-asked-questions/.html:
How do I get started?

Start with a complimentary consultation. We will talk briefly about what you are looking for and help determine which member of our Care Team may be the best fit.

Schedule a Complimentary Consultation

Do you offer in-person and virtual counseling?

Yes. LifeWise offers secure telehealth sessions throughout Texas and in-person counseling in select locations.

Do you accept insurance?

Yes. Insurance participation varies by provider and plan.

View Pricing and Insurance

What if I am not sure which counselor to choose?

That is exactly what the consultation is for. We can help you determine which provider may be the best fit based on your needs, preferences, availability, and payment options.

What types of counseling do you provide?

We provide individual, couples, and family counseling for adults with concerns including trauma, anxiety, relationships, neurodivergence, life transitions, and other emotional or behavioral health concerns.

Do you work with first responders and veterans?

Yes. We provide trauma-informed counseling for first responders, veterans, military members, dispatchers, and their families.

We also offer nonclinical resilience and mental readiness training through Steel Armor Mindset.

Explore First Responder Options

Do I have to talk about my trauma in detail?

No. Counseling does not require you to relive or describe traumatic experiences before you are ready. Treatment can focus on stabilization, regulation, coping skills, patterns, and current concerns.

What happens during the first session?

Your first session is an opportunity to talk about what brings you to counseling, what you would like to change, and what you need from your counselor. You do not need to arrive with everything figured out.

How long are counseling sessions?

Most counseling sessions are approximately 50 to 60 minutes.

What if LifeWise is not the right fit?

If we believe another provider or level of care would better meet your needs, we will be honest about that and may recommend other options when appropriate.

How do I cancel or reschedule?

Please provide at least 24 hours notice whenever possible. Cancellation and no-show policies vary depending on the provider and payment arrangement.

Is LifeWise a crisis service?

No. LifeWise does not provide emergency or crisis response services.

If you are experiencing an immediate emergency, call 911.

You may also call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

First responders may contact COPLINE at 1-800-COPLINE.

Veterans may call 988 and press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line.

Support Beyond LifeWise

Mental health care does not always happen in one office.

LifeWise Counseling and Wellness works hard to build relationships with trusted professionals and organizations that provide services outside the scope of our practice. These referral partners may offer additional support when clients need psychiatric care, medication management, a higher level of treatment, specialized services, or nonclinical coaching.

When clinically appropriate and with the client’s consent, we work collaboratively with our referral partners to support continuity of care, strengthen communication, and provide thoughtful, coordinated care for our clients.

Coaching and Personal Development

Brian Carlson provides nonclinical life coaching for individuals, adolescents, parents, and families seeking support with personal growth, relationships, parenting, life balance, goals, and overall wellness.

Services include individual coaching, group coaching, webinars, and other educational and personal development services.

Please note: Life coaching is not psychotherapy and does not replace mental health treatment when clinical care is needed.

Visit Brian Carlson

Psychiatry and Medication Management

Shiloh Health

Shiloh Health is an integrative psychiatry practice serving children, adolescents, and adults. Their approach combines psychiatric care with consideration of lifestyle, physical health, and other factors that may affect mental wellness.

Services include psychiatric evaluations, medication management, psychotherapy, lifestyle coaching, and additional integrative services.

Visit Shiloh Health

Pine Psychiatric Care Services provides psychiatric services for children, adolescents, and adults ages six and older in Texas.

Services include psychiatric assessment and evaluation, medication management and treatment, and supportive therapy, with an emphasis on individualized care and consideration of biological, psychological, and social factors.

Visit Pine Psychiatric

Higher Levels of Care

Pathlight Mood and Anxiety Center | Fort Worth| Dallas

Pathlight provides higher levels of mental health care for adults experiencing mood, anxiety, trauma related, and other behavioral health concerns.

The Fort Worth location offers Partial Hospitalization and Intensive Outpatient treatment, providing additional structure and clinical support for individuals whose needs extend beyond traditional outpatient counseling.

Visit Pathlight

The Hambrick Center for Counseling and Biofeedback

The Hambrick Center provides a mental health Intensive Outpatient Program for adolescents and adults who need more structured support than traditional weekly counseling but do not require inpatient hospitalization.

Their program includes group therapy, individual support, mental health education, care coordination, and individualized treatment planning for concerns including depression, anxiety, trauma, and PTSD.

Visit the Hambrick Center

Finding the Right Support

Not sure what type of care you need?

LifeWise can help you determine whether outpatient counseling with our Care Team may be appropriate or whether another level or type of service should be considered.

Schedule a Complimentary Consultation

Referral Disclaimer

LifeWise Counseling and Wellness provides referral information as a resource to clients and the community. Referral partners are independent professionals and organizations and are not employees, contractors, or agents of LifeWise Counseling and Wellness.

You don’t have to face it alone

When anxiety or depression show up, life can start to feel overwhelming, heavy, or out of control. You may feel stuck, exhausted, disconnected from the life you want.

Therapy can help you understand what you’re experiencing and find a way forward.

Depression does not always look like sadness. Sometimes it looks like exhaustion, withdrawal, numbness, or moving through the day without feeling fully present.

Sometimes the symptom is only part of the story

Anxiety and depression can develop alongside chronic stress, trauma, burnout, grief, relationship difficulties, neurodivergence, or major life changes.

Counseling can help you understand what is happening beneath the symptoms and identify patterns that may be keeping you stuck.

/neurodivergence/.title: Neurodivergence
/neurodivergence/.html:
You should not have to work this hard to fit

Neurodivergence can affect how you process information, manage attention, regulate emotions, communicate, organize daily life, and move through relationships or work.

You may have spent years adapting, masking, overcompensating, or wondering why things that seem easy for other people require so much effort.

Counseling can help you better understand your patterns, reduce shame, and build a life that works with your brain instead of constantly against it.

Find Support

Masking
Overwhelm

Emotional intensity
Feeling misunderstood

Neurodivergence does not always look obvious. Sometimes it looks like appearing capable on the outside while using enormous amounts of energy just to keep up.

When neurodivergence shows up

Daily life can become exhausting when your environment constantly demands more regulation, organization, flexibility, or social energy than your nervous system comfortably has available.

Sometimes the problem is not the person

Many neurodivergent adults have spent years being told they are too much, not trying hard enough, overly sensitive, disorganized, difficult, or inconsistent.

Counseling can help separate who you are from the expectations you learned to carry.

How counseling can help

Understand Your Patterns
Learn how attention, sensory needs, emotions, and executive functioning affect your daily life.

Reduce Masking
Explore where you have learned to hide, perform, or suppress parts of yourself.

Build Practical Strategies
Develop systems that actually fit the way you think and function.

Strengthen Self Understanding
Replace confusion and self criticism with greater clarity and self awareness.

Therapy that fits the person

Our providers work with neurodivergent adults experiencing concerns related to ADHD, anxiety, depression, trauma, relationships, burnout, identity, and major life transitions.

The goal is not to make you function more like everyone else. It is to help you understand what works for you and build from there.

/trauma/.title: Trauma
/trauma/.html:
When the past keeps showing up in the present

Trauma can affect the way you think, feel, connect with others, and respond to stress long after the experience itself has ended.

You may feel constantly on guard, emotionally numb, easily overwhelmed, disconnected from yourself, or unsure why certain situations affect you so strongly.

Counseling can help you make sense of those patterns and begin responding from the present instead of from survival mode.

Find Support

Trauma can look like

Hypervigilance
Emotional numbness
Intrusive memories
Nightmares
Avoidance
Irritability
Difficulty trusting others
Feeling disconnected
Shame or self blame
Strong emotional reactions
Relationship difficulties
Trouble feeling safe
Sleep problems
Feeling stuck in survival mode

Trauma does not always look like a crisis

Some trauma is obvious. Other experiences are harder to recognize because they happened gradually, repeatedly, or within relationships that were supposed to feel safe.

Trauma can develop after a single event, repeated exposure, chronic stress, loss, abuse, violence, neglect, betrayal, or experiences that overwhelmed your ability to cope at the time.

What matters is not whether your experience fits someone else’s definition of trauma. What matters is how it continues to affect you.

When trauma shows uP

Trauma can make the nervous system respond to present day situations as though danger is still happening.

A conversation, sound, conflict, memory, smell, location, or relationship dynamic may trigger a reaction that feels much bigger than the moment itself.

These responses are often attempts to protect you, even when they are no longer helping.

Trauma can look different in high stress roles

First responders, veterans, military members, dispatchers, and others in high stress roles may experience trauma differently because of repeated exposure, responsibility, and the expectation to keep functioning.

Common experiences can include hypervigilance, emotional detachment, irritability, difficulty transitioning out of work mode, sleep disruption, and feeling disconnected from family or everyday life.

For more specialized support, visit our First Responders and Veterans page.

Explore First Responder Resilience Support

How counseling can help

Understand Your Responses
Learn how past experiences may be influencing your emotions, thoughts, relationships, and reactions today.

Build a Sense of Safety
Develop practical ways to manage overwhelm and help your nervous system settle.

Recognize Patterns
Explore avoidance, hypervigilance, emotional shutdown, people pleasing, anger, or other patterns that developed as ways to cope.

Reconnect With Yourself
Build greater trust in yourself, strengthen boundaries, and create more room for connection, choice, and stability.

Trauma can affect relationships too

Trauma often changes how safe it feels to trust, depend on others, communicate needs, tolerate conflict, or allow yourself to be vulnerable.

You may find yourself withdrawing, becoming defensive, overexplaining, shutting down, or constantly watching for signs that something is wrong.

Counseling can help you understand these patterns without reducing them to character flaws.

You do not have to tell the whole story at once

Trauma counseling does not require you to immediately describe every painful experience in detail.

You can begin with what is happening now.

The pace of counseling should allow enough safety, trust, and stability for deeper work to happen when you are ready.

You are more than what happened to you

You may not be able to change what happened, but you can change the role it continues to play in your life.

You do not need to have the right words or know exactly where to begin.

/relationships/.title: Relationships
/relationships/.html:
When connection starts to feel hard

Relationships can be deeply meaningful and deeply complicated. Conflict, disconnection, resentment, betrayal, changing roles, or simply feeling misunderstood can leave people wondering how to move forward.

Counseling can help you slow down the pattern, understand what is happening underneath it, and build a healthier way of relating.

Find Support

Relationship difficulties can look like

Conflict that keeps repeating
Difficulty communicating
Feeling unheard or misunderstood
Emotional distance
Loss of trust
Resentment
Difficulty setting boundaries
Different expectations or needs
Feeling disconnected
Struggling to repair after conflict

Sometimes the argument is not really the argument

Many relationship conflicts are less about the surface issue and more about what happens underneath it. One person may feel dismissed, rejected, controlled, criticized, or alone while the other feels overwhelmed, misunderstood, or unsure how to respond.

Over time, couples and families can become trapped in patterns where both people are reacting to the pattern itself.

When relationships become strained

Stress, trauma, parenting, work demands, grief, major life changes, neurodivergence, differences in communication style, and unresolved hurt can all affect connection.

You may care deeply about the relationship and still feel stuck in ways that are difficult to change on your own.

How counseling can help

Understand the pattern
Identify what happens before, during, and after conflict so you can begin changing the cycle instead of repeating it.

Improve communication
Learn how to express needs, listen more effectively, and have difficult conversations without escalating or shutting down.

Rebuild trust
Work through hurt, resentment, betrayal, or disconnection with greater clarity and accountability.

Strengthen boundaries
Develop healthier expectations around responsibility, emotional labor, privacy, family, and individual needs.

Reconnect
Create more space for emotional safety, affection, understanding, and shared meaning.

Couples, families, and individuals

Relationship counseling is not limited to couples.

Individual counseling can also help when you are trying to understand your own patterns, strengthen boundaries, recover from a difficult relationship, or decide what you want moving forward.

Family counseling can help address communication problems, changing roles, conflict, and patterns that affect the family as a whole.

The goal is not to eliminate conflict

Healthy relationships still have disagreements.

The goal is to understand each other more clearly, respond with greater intention, repair when things go wrong, and build patterns that allow the relationship to feel safer and more connected.

A place to start

You do not have to wait until a relationship is in crisis before asking for help.

If communication has become harder, conflict keeps repeating, or the relationship no longer feels the way you want it to, counseling can create space to understand what needs to change.

Schedule a 15 minute consultation.

/stress/.title: Stress
/stress/.html:
When everything feels like too much

Stress is part of life, but when it becomes constant, your mind and body may never get a real chance to recover. You may feel overwhelmed, irritable, exhausted, scattered, or like you are always trying to catch up.

Therapy can help you understand what is keeping your system under pressure and find healthier ways to respond.

Find Support

Stress can feel like:
Irritability
Mental overload
Muscle tension
Trouble sleeping
Difficulty focusing
Feeling stretched too thin
Emotional exhaustion
Trouble slowing down
Feeling constantly responsible
Difficulty recovering

When stress becomes chronic

Ongoing stress can affect more than your mood. It can interfere with sleep, concentration, relationships, decision making, and your ability to feel present in your own life.

Sometimes the pressure comes from work, caregiving, relationships, major life changes, demanding roles, or simply carrying too much for too long.

You may notice

  • Difficulty slowing down
  • Feeling constantly responsible for everything
  • Being easily frustrated or emotionally reactive
  • Trouble concentrating or making decisions
  • Headaches, muscle tension, or physical exhaustion
  • Difficulty sleeping even when you are tired
  • Feeling disconnected from people you care about
  • Losing patience with things that normally would not bother you
  • Feeling guilty when you try to rest

Sometimes stress is doing more than wearing you out

When your body stays in a prolonged state of alert, even small demands can begin to feel bigger than they are. You may find yourself reacting quickly, shutting down, avoiding things, or pushing yourself harder just to keep functioning.

Counseling can help you recognize these patterns and understand what your mind and body are responding to.

How counseling can help

Understand what is driving the stress
Identify the situations, expectations, relationships, or patterns that are creating ongoing pressure.

Learn how to regulate your response
Develop practical ways to reduce physical and emotional overwhelm.

Create healthier boundaries
Recognize where your time, energy, and responsibilities may have become unsustainable.

Respond instead of react
Build greater awareness of your stress patterns so you have more choice in how you respond.

Make room for recovery
Learn how to rest and reconnect without feeling as though you should always be doing something.

Stress does not mean you are failing

Sometimes stress is simply your system telling you that the demands have exceeded the resources available to meet them.

Therapy can help you sort through what can change, what cannot, and how to protect your energy without withdrawing from the parts of life that matter to you.

A place to start

You do not have to wait until you are completely burned out before asking for support.

If stress has started affecting your mood, relationships, sleep, work, or ability to enjoy your life, it may be time to talk with someone.

Schedule a 15 minute consultation.

/life-challenges/.html:
When life does not go the way you expected

Life can change quickly. A loss, transition, new responsibility, difficult decision, or season of uncertainty can leave you feeling overwhelmed, disconnected, or unsure of what comes next.

Counseling can give you space to sort through what is happening and figure out how you want to move forward.

Find Support

Life challenges can look like

Major life transitions
Grief and loss
Career changes
Caregiving stress
Relationship changes
Parenting challenges
Identity shifts
Difficult decisions
Feeling stuck or directionless
Adjusting to unexpected change

Sometimes the hardest part is not knowing what comes next

You may be dealing with something you never planned for, or you may simply feel that the life you have no longer fits the way it once did.

Even positive changes can bring stress, uncertainty, and a sense of loss for what used to feel familiar.

When life starts to feel unfamiliar

Changes in work, family, relationships, health, responsibilities, or identity can affect the way you see yourself and the future.

You may find yourself questioning decisions, second guessing what you want, or trying to hold everything together while quietly feeling overwhelmed.

How counseling can help

Make sense of what is changing
Create space to understand what this season means for you and what may need your attention.

Process loss and uncertainty
Work through grief, disappointment, fear, or the emotional impact of unexpected change.

Clarify what matters
Identify your priorities, values, needs, and the direction you want to move toward.

Adjust to new roles
Explore how changes in relationships, work, family, or responsibility may be affecting your sense of self.

Move forward with intention
Develop practical steps for navigating uncertainty without feeling pressured to have everything figured out.

You do not need a diagnosis to benefit from counseling

Sometimes people come to counseling because something is wrong.

Other times, life has simply become complicated.

You may need a place to think, process, adjust, or decide what you want next. That is enough.

A place to start

You do not have to have the answer before you begin.

Counseling can help you make sense of where you are, what has changed, and what you want the next chapter to look like.

Schedule a 15 minute consultation.

No website, email system, text service, or internet transmission can be guaranteed completely secure. The Federal Trade Commission recommends collecting only necessary personal information, protecting retained information, disposing of it appropriately, and maintaining a response plan for security incidents.

Information that becomes part of a counseling record will be maintained according to applicable clinical recordkeeping and privacy requirements rather than this Website Privacy Policy.

Children’s Privacy

The federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Rule places specific requirements on websites directed to children under 13 or those that knowingly collect their personal information.

Professional Credentials

Licensed Professional Counselor

A Licensed Professional Counselor (LPC) is a mental health professional licensed by the Texas Behavioral Health Executive Council to provide professional counseling services. LPCs have completed required graduate education, examination, and supervised clinical experience and may practice independently within the scope of their license, education, training, and professional competence.

Licensed Professional Counselor Supervisor

A Licensed Professional Counselor Supervisor (LPC-S) is a Texas Licensed Professional Counselor who has met additional requirements to provide clinical supervision to LPC Associates working toward independent licensure. An LPC-S may provide professional counseling services independently and may also provide clinical supervision, consultation, and professional development within the scope of their license, training, and competence.

Licensed Professional Counselor Associate

A Licensed Professional Counselor Associate (LPC Associate) is a mental health professional licensed by the Texas Behavioral Health Executive Council who has completed the required graduate education and examination requirements for licensure and is completing the supervised clinical experience required for independent practice. LPC Associates provide professional counseling services under the supervision of a Texas LPC-S and practice within the scope of their license, education, training, and supervision.

Master’s Level Counseling Intern

A Master’s Level Counseling Intern is a graduate student completing the clinical training requirements of a master’s degree program in counseling or a related field. Counseling interns are not independently licensed and provide services as part of their supervised educational and clinical training. Their work is conducted under appropriate clinical and academic supervision and within the scope of their education, training, supervision, and applicable program requirements.

/2026/10/01/why-counselors-need-therapy-.title: Why Counselors Need Therapy Too
/2026/10/01/why-counselors-need-therapy-.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

Counselors spend a lot of time helping other people understand themselves.

We listen.

We notice patterns.

We sit with grief, fear, trauma, shame, anger, relationship problems, and all the complicated parts of being human.

And somehow, there can still be this strange idea that counselors should have their own lives completely figured out.

We do not.

Counselors are people first.

We have families, stress, histories, insecurities, losses, blind spots, relationships, bad days, and sometimes our own very well organized emotional baggage.

Clinical training does not make someone immune to being human.

Knowing the Tools Is Not the Same as Using Them

Counselors may know exactly what grounding is.

We may understand cognitive distortions, attachment patterns, emotional regulation, trauma responses, and boundaries.

That does not mean we are always able to recognize those things clearly in ourselves.

There is a big difference between understanding something intellectually and experiencing it personally.

We can know that reassurance seeking feeds anxiety and still want reassurance.

We can teach boundaries and still struggle to set one with someone we love.

We can recognize avoidance in a client while quietly avoiding something in our own life.

Insight helps.

It does not eliminate vulnerability.

Counselors Have Blind Spots Too

It is much easier to see patterns from outside the system.

When we are emotionally involved, our perspective changes.

Personal therapy gives counselors a space where they do not have to be the observer, helper, or professional in the room.

Someone else gets to ask the questions.

Someone else gets to notice the patterns.

Someone else gets to say, “Have you considered that this might be about you?”

That kind of reflection can be uncomfortable.

It can also be incredibly useful.

The Work Can Affect Us

Counselors regularly hear stories involving trauma, abuse, grief, violence, betrayal, loss, and human suffering.

Being trained to hold those stories does not mean they have no impact.

Over time, counselors can experience compassion fatigue, burnout, secondary traumatic stress, or emotional exhaustion.

Therapy can provide a place to process what belongs to us, what belongs to the work, and where the two may be starting to overlap.

That matters because unprocessed emotional material does not disappear simply because someone has a license hanging on the wall.

Our Personal History Comes Into the Room

Every counselor has a history.

Our experiences shape how we understand relationships, conflict, family, success, failure, safety, trust, and vulnerability.

Good clinicians work hard to remain aware of how their own experiences may influence their reactions to clients.

Therapy can help us identify triggers, unresolved wounds, assumptions, and emotional reactions before they begin influencing the clinical relationship.

This is not about becoming perfectly healed before helping anyone else.

There is no such thing.

It is about developing enough self awareness to recognize when our own story is getting louder than the client’s.

Therapy Gives Counselors a Place to Stop Performing

Counselors spend much of their professional lives paying attention to someone else.

Personal therapy creates a rare space where the focus can shift.

We do not have to have the answer.

We do not have to be regulated for someone else.

We do not have to translate our feelings into something clinically useful.

We can simply be a person having a hard time.

That alone can be valuable.

A Simple Reflection

For counselors, helpers, caregivers, and anyone who spends a lot of time supporting others, consider:

Where do I go when I am the one who needs support?

What emotions am I good at helping other people tolerate but tend to avoid in myself?

Am I processing my stress, or am I simply functioning through it?

When was the last time I had a space where I did not have to take care of anyone else?

Sometimes the people who are best at holding space for others forget that they need somewhere to put their own things down.

Therapy Is Not Evidence That a Counselor Is Struggling Professionally

In many cases, it is evidence that they take self awareness seriously.

Therapists do not need to be perfect.

They need to be reflective, ethical, emotionally aware, and willing to examine themselves.

The goal is not to become a person who never struggles.

The goal is to become someone who notices when they are struggling and knows when to seek support.

Counselors need therapy for many of the same reasons everyone else does.

Because we are human too.

/2026/09/24/we-created-our-identity/.title: We create our identity
/2026/09/24/we-created-our-identity/.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

A lot of people reach a point in life where they ask:

Who am I, really?

Sometimes that question shows up after a breakup, a career change, becoming a parent, losing a relationship, leaving a controlling family system, or simply realizing that most of your life has been shaped by what other people expected from you.

For some people, identity feels less like something they chose and more like something they inherited.

The responsible one.

The difficult one.

The achiever.

The caretaker.

The peacemaker.

The strong one.

The disappointment.

The funny one.

The problem.

Over time, those roles can start to feel permanent.

But they are not.

Identity Is Not Just Something You Discover

We often talk about “finding yourself” as if there is one perfectly formed version of you hidden somewhere, waiting to be uncovered.

Identity is usually more active than that.

We create it.

We shape it through our choices, values, boundaries, relationships, habits, and the meaning we make from our experiences.

You may not have chosen everything that happened to you.

You may not have chosen the labels other people gave you.

But as an adult, you can begin deciding which parts still belong.

Other People Help Shape Us

Our early identity is often heavily influenced by family.

Children learn quickly who they are “supposed” to be.

Maybe you were praised for being easygoing, so you learned not to have needs.

Maybe mistakes were heavily criticized, so you learned that being wrong meant being a failure.

Maybe keeping the peace became your job.

Maybe achievement became the way you earned approval.

Those adaptations may have made sense at the time.

The problem comes when an old survival role becomes an adult identity.

At some point, you get to ask:

Do I actually believe this about myself, or was I taught to believe it?

You Are More Than Your Past

Your history matters.

It influences how you see yourself, what you fear, what you expect from relationships, and how you respond to stress.

But your past is not a permanent job description.

You are allowed to become more assertive even if you were once the quiet one.

You are allowed to change careers.

You are allowed to disappoint people.

You are allowed to stop being the fixer.

You are allowed to discover that something you once valued no longer fits.

Growth often involves becoming unfamiliar to people who were comfortable with the old version of you.

That can feel unsettling.

It can also be necessary.

Start With Values, Not Labels

When people feel lost, they often ask, “What kind of person am I?”

A more useful question can be:

What kind of person do I want to practice being?

Maybe you want to be honest.

Present.

Curious.

Reliable.

Playful.

Independent.

Compassionate.

Courageous.

You do not have to feel like that person before you begin acting like that person.

Identity is strengthened through repetition.

If you want to become someone who speaks up, practice speaking up.

If you want to become someone who protects their time, practice boundaries.

If you want to become someone who is more present in relationships, practice returning your attention when it wanders.

Small choices become evidence.

And eventually, those choices begin to change the story you tell yourself about who you are.

A Simple Reflection Exercise

Take a few minutes and finish these sentences:

I learned that I was supposed to be:
Write down the roles, labels, or expectations you grew up with.

The parts of that identity that still feel true are:
Keep what genuinely fits.

The parts I am ready to question or release are:
Notice what may belong more to your past than your present.

The person I want to practice becoming is someone who:
Choose two or three qualities that reflect your values.

Then ask yourself:

What is one small choice I can make this week that supports that version of me?

Identity changes through repeated choices, not one dramatic reinvention.

You Are Allowed to Edit the Story

One of the most powerful parts of adulthood is realizing that identity is not a finished document.

You can revise it.

You can keep the parts that feel true.

You can question the parts that were handed to you.

You can let go of roles that no longer fit.

You can become someone your younger self would not recognize.

That is not being fake.

That is growth.

You are not required to remain the person you became in order to survive earlier chapters of your life.

You get to participate in who you become next.

/2026/09/17/wet-socks-sitting-with-disco.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

There are few things more irritating than wet socks.

They are not catastrophic. They are not dangerous. But they are uncomfortable enough that your brain wants them fixed immediately.

Change the socks. Find a dry pair. Make the sensation stop.

That little urge captures something important about how we often respond to emotional discomfort too.

We want relief.

We want the anxiety gone, the sadness lifted, the uncertainty resolved, the rejection explained, the conflict settled, the awkward feeling erased.

And when discomfort shows up, many of us immediately move toward something that will make it stop.

We avoid.

We overthink.

We distract.

We scroll.

We drink.

We seek reassurance.

We shut down.

We stay busy.

Sometimes we even try to control other people because their behavior is making us uncomfortable.

The problem is that constantly escaping discomfort can teach our nervous system that discomfort itself is dangerous.

It is not.

Discomfort Is Not the Same as Danger

This distinction matters.

Anxiety can feel intense without being dangerous.

Embarrassment can feel unbearable without actually being harmful.

Uncertainty can make us restless without meaning something bad is about to happen.

Sitting with discomfort means learning to notice an unpleasant feeling without immediately trying to eliminate it.

That does not mean ignoring real danger, tolerating mistreatment, or forcing yourself to stay in harmful situations.

It means learning the difference between:

“This is unsafe.”

and

“I really do not like how this feels.”

Those are not the same thing.

Why We Avoid Uncomfortable Feelings

Avoidance works beautifully in the short term.

If you cancel the event that makes you anxious, the anxiety drops.

If you ask for reassurance, you may feel calmer.

If you distract yourself every time sadness appears, you may get temporary relief.

Your brain notices that relief and says, “Excellent. Do that again.”

Over time, avoidance can make the original feeling even more powerful because you never get the opportunity to learn that you can tolerate it.

You become less afraid of the situation and more afraid of the feeling the situation creates.

What Does Sitting With Discomfort Actually Look Like?

It is usually much less dramatic than people imagine.

It might mean noticing anxiety and continuing the conversation anyway.

It might mean allowing someone to be disappointed with you without immediately fixing it.

It might mean feeling lonely without contacting someone who repeatedly hurts you.

It might mean making a mistake and resisting the urge to spend the next four hours mentally prosecuting yourself.

It might mean admitting:

“I feel uncomfortable right now, and I can handle being uncomfortable.”

You do not have to enjoy the feeling.

You do not have to approve of it.

You simply practice allowing it to exist without handing it the steering wheel.

Try the Wet Socks Exercise

The next time you notice yourself rushing to escape an uncomfortable emotion, ask yourself:

What am I feeling?

Name it as specifically as you can.

Is this dangerous, or is it uncomfortable?

If there is genuine danger, respond appropriately.

If it is discomfort, pause.

What am I tempted to do to make this feeling disappear?

Notice whether you want to avoid, control, reassure, numb, withdraw, or overthink.

Then ask:

Can I stay with this feeling for five more minutes before I react?

You are not promising to feel it forever.

You are simply giving your nervous system a chance to discover that discomfort rises, shifts, and eventually changes.

You Can Be Uncomfortable and Still Be Okay

Emotional regulation is not the ability to feel calm all the time.

It is the ability to experience difficult emotions without automatically becoming controlled by them.

Sometimes growth feels peaceful.

Sometimes growth feels like sitting in wet socks for a few minutes longer than you would prefer.

Uncomfortable?

Absolutely.

Impossible?

Usually not.

And every time you discover that you can tolerate a difficult feeling without immediately escaping it, you build a little more trust in yourself.

/2026/09/10/high-functioning-depression-.title: High Functioning Depression: What You Should Know
/2026/09/10/high-functioning-depression-.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP, Clinical Director of LifeWise Counseling

Social media has made mental health information more accessible, which can be helpful. But it has also made it easy to turn normal emotions into diagnoses without understanding the full clinical picture.

Feeling sad does not automatically mean someone has depression. Neither does feeling unmotivated, overwhelmed, or having a difficult week.

At the same time, depression does not always look like obvious sadness.

Someone can work, laugh, parent, socialize, succeed, and appear completely fine while struggling internally. So, what actually makes depression different?

Depression Is More Than Sadness

Sadness is a normal human emotion. It often follows disappointment, loss, conflict, rejection, or major life changes and usually shifts with time.

Clinical depression involves a broader pattern of emotional, cognitive, physical, and behavioral symptoms that persist and affect a person’s functioning.

Depression may include:

  1. Persistent sadness, emptiness, or low mood
  2. Loss of interest or pleasure in things once enjoyed
  3. Changes in sleep or appetite
  4. Fatigue or low energy
  5. Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt
  6. Difficulty concentrating or making decisions
  7. Feeling unusually restless or slowed down
  8. Irritability, withdrawal, or emotional numbness
  9. Recurrent thoughts of death or suicide

For Major Depressive Disorder, several symptoms are generally present during the same two week period and represent a noticeable change from the person’s usual functioning.

Depression Does Not Look the Same in Everyone

One person may struggle to get out of bed while another continues going to work every day.

One person may cry frequently while another feels almost nothing.

Some people isolate. Others become extremely busy and productive.

This is why appearance alone tells us very little about what someone may be experiencing internally.

What About “High Functioning Depression”?

“High functioning depression” is a commonly used phrase, but it is not an official diagnosis.

People often use it to describe someone who experiences depressive symptoms while continuing to manage work, family, relationships, and other responsibilities.

They may look successful and happy while privately feeling exhausted, disconnected, hopeless, or emotionally flat.

Depending on the symptoms and how long they have been present, a clinician may consider diagnoses such as Persistent Depressive Disorder or another depressive condition.

The important distinction is that being able to function does not necessarily mean someone is emotionally well.

Context Matters

Depression can also overlap with grief, anxiety, ADHD, trauma, burnout, medical conditions, hormonal changes, sleep problems, substance use, and major life transitions.

That is one reason a professional assessment involves more than checking symptoms off a list.

Clinicians consider how long symptoms have been present, how severe they are, what else may be contributing, and how significantly they are affecting someone’s life.

Social Media Can Educate, But It Cannot Diagnose

Recognizing yourself in a mental health post can be useful. It may help you put words to something you have been experiencing.

But relating to a symptom does not necessarily mean you have a disorder.

A better question may be:

“Has something changed in the way I feel, function, connect with others, or experience my life?”

If the answer is yes, especially if those changes have continued for several weeks, talking with a qualified mental health professional may help you better understand what is happening.

Mental health awareness is important.

So is mental health accuracy.

You do not need to diagnose yourself before asking for support.

LifeWise Counseling provides inclusive, evidence based counseling through telehealth across Texas, with in person services available in select areas.

If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide or believe you may be in immediate danger, call or text 988, call 911, or go to your nearest emergency department.

/2026/08/27/autism-is-not-a-personality-.title: Autism Is Not a Personality Type: Why Traits Are Not the Same as a Diagnosis
/2026/08/27/autism-is-not-a-personality-.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

Autism has become increasingly visible in conversations about mental health, neurodiversity, identity, and self understanding.

That visibility has done some genuinely useful things. More adults are recognizing lifelong patterns that were missed in childhood. Women, people of color, and individuals who learned to camouflage their difficulties have historically been underidentified. Awareness has helped some people finally seek an appropriate evaluation.

But there is another side to increased awareness.

Autism has also become unusually common language on social media.

You prefer routines? Autism.

You hate certain textures? Autism.

You rehearse conversations before having them? Autism.

You feel socially awkward? Autism.

You have a favorite topic you could discuss for hours? Autism.

You get overwhelmed at Costco?

Apparently the internet has already assembled the diagnostic team.

The problem is that autistic traits are not the same thing as Autism Spectrum Disorder.

And recognizing yourself in a social media post does not establish a diagnosis.

Autism Is a Neurodevelopmental Disorder

Autism Spectrum Disorder, or ASD, is classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder.

According to current diagnostic criteria, autism involves persistent differences or deficits in social communication and social interaction, along with restricted or repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. These symptoms originate during the developmental period, even if they do not become fully apparent until later demands exceed someone’s ability to compensate.

That developmental component matters.

Autism is not something that suddenly appears because you became burned out at 35.

It is not acquired because you experienced trauma.

It is not created by anxiety.

Someone may certainly reach adulthood without receiving a diagnosis, but an adult diagnosis still involves evaluating evidence of a developmental pattern that began much earlier in life.

Autism Has Specific Diagnostic Criteria

For someone to meet criteria for Autism Spectrum Disorder, clinicians are looking for much more than a collection of relatable characteristics.

The DSM framework requires persistent difficulties across all three areas of social communication and interaction, including social emotional reciprocity, nonverbal communication, and developing, maintaining, or understanding relationships.

There must also be at least two types of restricted or repetitive behavior, such as repetitive movements or speech, significant insistence on sameness, highly restricted interests, or unusual responses to sensory input.

Symptoms must also be significant enough to affect functioning.

That means a diagnosis is based on the overall developmental and functional pattern, not whether someone likes routines, dislikes fluorescent lighting, or has an intense interest in a television series.

Having Autism Traits Does Not Mean You Have Autism

This distinction gets lost constantly.

Many people have characteristics associated with autism.

You might:

  • Prefer routines
  • Become overwhelmed in loud environments
  • Need time alone after socializing
  • Have strong interests
  • Dislike small talk
  • Struggle with eye contact
  • Rehearse conversations
  • Become distressed by unexpected changes
  • Be sensitive to certain textures
  • Feel socially awkward
  • Need predictability
  • Engage in repetitive movements when anxious

Any one of those experiences can be completely real without meaning that you have Autism Spectrum Disorder.

Human characteristics exist on continua.

Having a trait associated with a disorder does not automatically mean you have the disorder.

Most people have experienced anxiety. Most people do not have an anxiety disorder.

Most people occasionally become distracted. Most people do not have ADHD.

Most people have habits or preferences. Most people do not have OCD.

The same principle applies to autism.

Many Autism Symptoms Overlap With Other Conditions

This is one reason self diagnosis becomes particularly unreliable.

Some characteristics commonly associated with autism can also occur with:

  • ADHD
  • PTSD and trauma responses
  • Social anxiety
  • Generalized anxiety
  • Obsessive Compulsive Disorder
  • Depression
  • Attachment difficulties
  • Sensory processing differences
  • Personality characteristics
  • Chronic stress
  • Burnout

Someone who avoids eye contact may be autistic.

They may also be anxious.

Someone who becomes highly distressed when plans change may have autism.

They may also have OCD, trauma related hypervigilance, anxiety, or simply a very strong preference for predictability.

Someone who feels exhausted after social interaction may be masking autistic traits.

They may also be introverted, socially anxious, depressed, traumatized, overstimulated, or exhausted.

Symptoms do not belong exclusively to diagnoses.

That is why differential diagnosis exists.

Social Media Is Very Good at Recognition and Very Bad at Differential Diagnosis

Social media algorithms are designed to show you more of what captures your attention.

Watch several videos about adult autism and suddenly your feed may begin explaining your entire personality through autism.

That does not mean an algorithm has discovered your diagnosis.

It means the algorithm discovered what keeps you watching.

Mental health content often presents traits without discussing their frequency, severity, developmental history, context, or overlap with other conditions.

Those details are inconvenient in a 30 second video.

They are also essential to diagnosis.

“Masking” Should Not Become an Explanation for Every Missing Symptom

Masking is a legitimate phenomenon.

Some autistic people consciously or unconsciously compensate for social communication differences, imitate expected behavior, suppress repetitive behavior, or develop strategies that allow them to navigate social environments.

This can contribute to later diagnosis, particularly among people whose autism was not recognized in childhood. Research and clinical discussions increasingly acknowledge that some adults, including many women, historically went unidentified.

But masking cannot become an unfalsifiable explanation where every absence of diagnostic evidence becomes evidence of autism.

“I do not appear to have this symptom because I mask it” cannot, by itself, establish that the symptom exists.

Good assessment still requires a careful developmental history and evaluation of the person’s broader pattern of functioning.

But What About Adults Who Were Never Diagnosed?

They absolutely exist.

Historically, autism was understood much more narrowly than it is today. Diagnostic criteria have changed, professional understanding has improved, awareness has increased, and clinicians have become better at identifying presentations that may have been missed previously.

Autism diagnoses have increased substantially over time. Current CDC surveillance estimates indicate that approximately 1 in 31 eight year old children in the United States has been identified with ASD.

An adult who was overlooked as a child may therefore reasonably wonder whether autism explains lifelong experiences.

Wondering is appropriate.

Exploring is appropriate.

Seeking an assessment is appropriate.

But wondering whether you have autism and having autism are not the same statement.

Self Identification Can Be the Beginning of an Evaluation, Not the End of One

People sometimes object to professional assessment because adult autism evaluations can be expensive, specialists may be difficult to find, and waiting lists can be long.

Those are legitimate barriers.

It is completely reasonable for someone to say:

“I suspect I may be autistic.”

“I recognize a lot of autistic traits in myself.”

“I would like to be evaluated for autism.”

Those statements leave room for exploration.

That is different from turning a suspicion into a definitive diagnosis.

If you have never undergone an appropriate evaluation, the most clinically accurate statement is that you suspect you may have autism, not that autism has been established.

Diagnosis Is More Than Validation

Sometimes people understandably want a diagnosis because it seems to explain experiences that previously felt confusing.

There can be enormous relief in finally finding language for lifelong struggles.

But the purpose of diagnosis is not simply to provide a validating identity.

A diagnosis should help clinicians understand:

  • What is happening
  • What is causing impairment
  • What other explanations need to be considered
  • What support may be useful
  • What treatment or accommodations may be appropriate

Sometimes an autism evaluation results in an autism diagnosis.

Sometimes it reveals ADHD.

Sometimes trauma.

Sometimes anxiety.

Sometimes several conditions occurring together.

And sometimes the evaluation determines that a person has autistic traits without meeting criteria for Autism Spectrum Disorder.

That information can still be useful.

A Diagnosis Does Not Make Someone More Legitimate

There is also an important distinction worth making.

Saying that autism requires appropriate diagnosis does not mean someone’s struggles are imaginary unless they qualify for ASD.

You can experience sensory overwhelm without autism.

You can struggle socially without autism.

You can need routines without autism.

You can become exhausted from masking aspects of your personality without autism.

You can need therapy, accommodations, boundaries, coping strategies, or greater self understanding without acquiring a diagnostic label first.

Your distress does not have to become a disorder in order to deserve attention.

Autism Is Not an Internet Identity Quiz

Mental health awareness becomes less useful when every recognizable human experience is converted into pathology.

Autism is real.

Autistic people deserve accurate diagnosis, appropriate accommodations, respect, and access to services.

Precisely because autism is real, we should be careful not to dilute the diagnosis until nearly every personality characteristic becomes evidence of it.

A TikTok video can introduce an idea.

A checklist can identify traits worth exploring.

A personal story can make someone feel seen.

None of those things can determine whether someone meets diagnostic criteria for Autism Spectrum Disorder.

The Bottom Line

You can have autistic traits without having autism.

You can relate strongly to autistic people without being autistic.

You can wonder whether you are autistic without knowing yet.

And you can discover autism in adulthood after an appropriate evaluation.

Those statements can all be true at the same time.

If you suspect you may have Autism Spectrum Disorder, consider discussing your concerns with a qualified professional who can evaluate your developmental history, current functioning, symptoms, and possible alternative explanations.

The goal should not be to prove that you have autism.

The goal should be to understand yourself accurately.

Because recognition is not diagnosis, and relatability is not a diagnostic criterion.

If You Are Struggling

If social difficulties, sensory overwhelm, trauma symptoms, anxiety, emotional regulation, or relationship patterns are interfering with your life, support is available whether or not those experiences ultimately result in a diagnosis.

A qualified mental health professional can help you explore what is happening and determine what type of support may be most useful.

/2026/08/20/dissociative-identity-disord.title: Dissociative Identity Disorder: What It Is, What It Is Not, and Why Most People Do Not Have It
/2026/08/20/dissociative-identity-disord.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

Dissociative Identity Disorder, commonly called DID, has become much more visible in popular culture and on social media. Increased awareness of mental health can be helpful. At the same time, short videos and symptom lists can make complex psychiatric conditions appear far more common and easier to identify than they actually are.

Having different sides of yourself does not mean you have DID.

Feeling disconnected does not mean you have DID.

Changing how you behave depending on who you are around does not mean you have DID.

And experiencing dissociation does not automatically mean you have DID.

DID is a specific and complex dissociative disorder that requires much more than feeling like you have different parts of yourself.

First, What Is Dissociation?

Dissociation exists on a spectrum.

At its simplest, dissociation involves a disruption in the normal integration of awareness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, or experience. Dissociative experiences can occur in people who do not have a dissociative disorder.

For example, you might:

  • Drive somewhere familiar and realize you remember very little of the drive.
  • Become so absorbed in a book, movie, or project that you temporarily lose awareness of your surroundings.
  • Feel emotionally numb during an overwhelming situation.
  • Feel detached from yourself when extremely anxious or stressed.
  • Experience moments when your surroundings seem strange or unreal.

Trauma survivors may experience dissociation more frequently, particularly when the nervous system perceives danger. Dissociative symptoms can also occur with PTSD, acute stress, panic, depression, anxiety, sleep deprivation, substance use, and other psychological or medical conditions.

In other words, dissociation is a symptom. DID is a diagnosis.

Those are not the same thing.

So What Is Dissociative Identity Disorder?

DID was previously called Multiple Personality Disorder. It is classified in the DSM 5 TR as a dissociative disorder, not a personality disorder.

A person with DID experiences a significant disruption of identity involving two or more distinct personality states. There are also recurrent gaps in memory that are beyond ordinary forgetfulness.

These disruptions may affect behavior, consciousness, memory, perception, cognition, sensory functioning, and the person’s sense of identity.

Importantly, the symptoms must cause significant distress or interfere with important areas of life. Clinicians must also consider cultural or religious practices, substances, neurological conditions, and other possible explanations before diagnosing DID.

Common Symptoms of DID

Someone with DID may experience:

  • Significant gaps in memory for everyday events
  • Missing memories for important personal information
  • Amnesia surrounding traumatic experiences
  • A sense that periods of time have disappeared
  • Evidence of actions or activities they do not remember completing
  • Significant changes in behavior or sense of self
  • Distinct identity states
  • Feeling that thoughts, emotions, actions, or impulses do not belong to them
  • Depersonalization, or feeling detached from oneself
  • Derealization, or feeling that the world around them is unreal
  • Confusion about identity
  • Significant emotional distress or difficulty functioning

The memory disturbance is particularly important. DID involves more than behaving differently from one situation to another.

DID Is Uncommon

Estimates vary depending on the population being studied and how the diagnosis is assessed. Clinical references estimate that approximately 1 to 1.5 percent of the general United States population may meet criteria for DID.

That means roughly 98 to 99 out of every 100 people do not have DID.

DID is real. People who genuinely live with the disorder deserve appropriate, compassionate treatment.

But recognizing that DID exists does not mean we should assume that every experience of dissociation, identity confusion, emotional change, or internal conflict represents DID.

Having “Parts” Does Not Mean You Have Multiple Identities

This is one of the most important distinctions.

Human beings are psychologically complex.

You may have a part of yourself that wants to succeed and another part that is terrified of failing.

You may be confident at work and insecure in relationships.

You might desperately want connection while simultaneously wanting everyone to leave you alone.

You may even talk internally to different parts of yourself.

None of those experiences automatically indicate DID.

Many therapeutic approaches intentionally use the language of “parts” to help people understand competing emotions, beliefs, needs, protective responses, and patterns of behavior.

Having internal parts is not equivalent to having separate dissociative identity states.

Mood Changes Are Not Identity Changes

Another common misunderstanding involves dramatic changes in mood.

Someone might say:

“I feel like a completely different person when I am angry.”

That can certainly feel intense.

But feeling different when angry, frightened, depressed, overwhelmed, or activated does not necessarily represent a separate identity.

Our nervous systems influence how we think, feel, remember, interpret situations, and behave.

A calm version of you may respond very differently from a terrified version of you.

Both can still be you.

Trauma Does Not Automatically Cause DID

DID is strongly associated clinically with severe and chronic trauma, particularly experiences occurring during childhood. Trauma and dissociation are closely connected, but most people who experience trauma do not develop DID.

Trauma can contribute to many different responses, including:

  • PTSD
  • Anxiety
  • Depression
  • Emotional numbing
  • Hypervigilance
  • Panic
  • Avoidance
  • Attachment difficulties
  • Memory problems
  • Depersonalization
  • Derealization
  • Other dissociative symptoms

Two people can survive similar experiences and develop entirely different psychological responses.

The nervous system is complicated. It rarely reads the diagnostic manual before deciding how it is going to cope.

Why Self Diagnosis Can Be Misleading

Many mental health symptoms overlap.

Memory difficulties can occur with ADHD, depression, PTSD, sleep problems, medications, neurological conditions, chronic stress, and substance use.

Feeling unreal can happen during panic attacks.

Emotional shifts can occur with trauma responses, anxiety, mood disorders, attachment patterns, or ordinary human stress.

Feeling like you have different versions of yourself can occur without any mental health disorder at all.

This is why clinicians do not diagnose DID based on one interesting symptom or an online checklist.

Assessment involves looking at the pattern, severity, duration, context, functional impairment, memory disturbance, trauma history, differential diagnoses, and alternative explanations.

Social Media Can Flatten Complicated Diagnoses

Mental health content online has helped many people develop language for experiences they previously could not explain.

That is valuable.

The problem begins when education quietly turns into diagnosis.

A thirty second video cannot tell you whether you have DID.

Neither can relating strongly to someone’s story.

Neither can having several symptoms from a checklist.

Psychiatric diagnoses are patterns, not personality quizzes.

When we reduce complex conditions to catchy symptom lists, ordinary experiences can begin to look pathological, while the experiences of people living with severe disorders may actually become less understood.

“I Relate to This” Is Not the Same as “I Have This”

You can relate deeply to information about a disorder without having that disorder.

You may recognize dissociation.

You may recognize trauma responses.

You may recognize internal conflict.

You may recognize emotional shifts or memory difficulties.

Those experiences are worth exploring.

They simply do not tell us, by themselves, what diagnosis explains them.

A better question than “Do I have DID?” may sometimes be:

“What is happening to me, when does it happen, what function might it be serving, and how much is it affecting my life?”

That question gives us considerably more room to understand the person rather than chasing a label.

When to Seek Professional Evaluation

Consider talking with a qualified mental health professional if you experience significant memory gaps, unexplained periods of lost time, persistent depersonalization or derealization, severe identity disturbance, substantial changes in behavior you cannot remember, or dissociative symptoms that interfere with your relationships, work, safety, or daily functioning.

The goal of assessment should not be proving that you have a particular diagnosis.

The goal should be understanding what is happening and determining what type of treatment might actually help.

The Bottom Line

Dissociation is real.

Dissociative Identity Disorder is real.

They are not interchangeable.

Most people occasionally disconnect, compartmentalize, behave differently in different environments, experience competing internal parts, or feel unlike themselves when emotionally overwhelmed.

Most people do not have DID.

Accurate mental health education requires us to hold two ideas at the same time:

We should take DID seriously without making it commonplace.

And we should take someone’s distress seriously even when DID is not the explanation.

Because ultimately, good mental health care is not about finding the most dramatic name for what someone is experiencing.

It is about understanding the person accurately enough to help.

If You Are Struggling

If dissociation, trauma symptoms, anxiety, or emotional distress are interfering with your life, support is available. A qualified mental health professional can help you understand what you are experiencing and develop a treatment plan based on your individual needs.

/2026/08/11/building-tolerance-for-uncer.title: Building Tolerance for Uncertainty: A Step-by-Step Guide
/2026/08/11/building-tolerance-for-uncer.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

One of the biggest challenges in life is uncertainty. When we cannot predict an outcome, we often try to control it instead. That need for control can show up in our relationships, our work, our family life, our habits, and even in the way we manage our emotions.

Uncertainty can trigger fear, especially fear of the unknown. Our minds do not always like unanswered questions, and when we do not know what is going to happen, our nervous systems may respond as though we are facing a threat.

We may become anxious, tense, stressed, or emotionally dysregulated. Some people run from uncertainty. Some become combative. Some become clingy, while others freeze or shut down. We may keep ourselves constantly busy so we do not have to deal with what we are afraid of. We may become impulsive, engage in risky behaviors, overthink every possible outcome, seek constant reassurance, or crawl into bed and sleep far more than usual between crying sessions.

These responses may look very different on the surface, but they often have something in common: they are attempts to escape, reduce, or control the discomfort of not knowing.

The problem is that uncertainty is unavoidable. We cannot predict every outcome, prevent every loss, control every relationship, or guarantee that things will work out the way we hope.

So, if uncertainty is something we cannot eliminate, what can we do about it?

A Plan of Action for Managing Uncertainty

The goal is not to eliminate uncertainty. That is impossible. The goal is to become more capable of tolerating the discomfort that comes with not knowing.

Start by noticing what uncertainty is making you want to do.

  • Are you seeking reassurance?
  • Trying to control another person?
  • Overthinking every possible outcome?
  • Staying excessively busy?
  • Avoiding something altogether?
  • Becoming reactive, impulsive, or emotionally shut down?

Once you recognize the pattern, pause before automatically responding to it.

1. Identify what you actually know.
Separate facts from fears, predictions, assumptions, and worst case scenarios. Ask yourself, “What do I know right now?” You may discover that much of your distress is coming from what might happen rather than what is actually happening.

2. Identify what is within your control.
You may not be able to control the outcome, another person’s choices, or what happens next. You can usually control how you respond, what boundaries you set, what information you seek, and what action you take today.

3. Regulate before you problem solve.
An activated nervous system is not especially good at making thoughtful decisions. Slow your breathing, move your body, take a walk, use grounding skills, step away from the situation, or do something that helps your body settle. Regulation does not solve the uncertainty. It helps you respond to it more effectively.

4. Stop feeding the reassurance cycle.
Reassurance may help temporarily, but repeatedly checking, asking, researching, monitoring, or seeking confirmation can actually strengthen anxiety over time. Before checking again, ask yourself whether you genuinely need new information or whether you are trying to make an uncomfortable feeling disappear.

5. Choose one useful action.
If there is something practical you can do, do it. Send the email. Make the appointment. Create the budget. Have the conversation. Gather the necessary information. Then stop. More thinking does not always produce more control.

6. Practice allowing the unanswered question to remain unanswered.
Sometimes the healthiest response really is, “I do not know yet.” That can feel uncomfortable without being dangerous. Give yourself opportunities to experience uncertainty without immediately fixing, avoiding, or neutralizing it.

7. Return to the present.
Anxiety tends to pull us into an imagined future. Ask yourself what requires your attention today. Not next month. Not every possible outcome. Today.

Over time, tolerating uncertainty becomes less about convincing yourself that everything will be fine and more about developing confidence that you can handle what happens next.

That is a very different kind of security. It does not come from knowing the future. It comes from trusting your ability to respond to it.

If you or someone you care about is struggling with anxiety, uncertainty, emotional overwhelm, or simply feeling stuck, you do not have to figure it out alone. The LifeWise Counseling and Wellness Care Team is here to help you understand what is happening, develop practical tools, and find a healthier way forward.

/2026/07/30/lessons-ive-learned-from-my-.title: Lessons I’ve learned from my parents and from being a parent
/2026/07/30/lessons-ive-learned-from-my-.html:
By Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

I think most of us can look back at the way our parents navigated both parenting and life and recognize that we’ve learned something from them. Some of those lessons are ones we’re grateful for. Others taught us what we don’t want to repeat. Either way, every experience holds value if we’re willing to learn from it.

Parenting has also taught me lessons that continued long after my child was grown. Looking back, I’m grateful for both perspectives because each has shaped the person, parent, and therapist I am today.

From My Parents

  • Suppressing emotions often leads to anger, anxiety, depression, relationship difficulties, feeling unseen or unloved, and countless other struggles.
  • Sometimes children are more emotionally mature than their parents.
  • Unhealed generational wounds are often passed down until someone chooses to break the cycle.
  • Just because someone is family doesn’t mean they are emotionally or physically safe.
  • Living from fear and conformity is not the only way to live.
  • Being part of someone’s life is a privilege, not a birthright.
  • Beliefs should cultivate compassion, wisdom, and integrity rather than fear or shame.
  • Parents are meant to protect their children from abusive adults.
  • Parents are meant to comfort their children, not dismiss their emotions.
  • Children are supposed to cry. Tears are not a sign of weakness.
  • Untreated trauma and undiagnosed or undertreated mental health conditions can affect families for generations.
  • Siblings don’t always become lifelong friends. Sometimes they become our greatest source of pain.
  • Silence doesn’t heal wounds. Avoiding difficult conversations doesn’t make the pain disappear.
  • Parents are human beings too. They have their own trauma, limitations, and healing to do.

From Being a Parent

  • Sometimes children are more emotionally mature than their parents.
  • We learn the most when we’re willing to truly listen to our children.
  • Teaching children to think critically prepares them far better for life than teaching them what to think.
  • Our children deserve autonomy, their own opinions, and the freedom to make choices that differ from ours.
  • Our children may develop values that are different from our own, and that is part of becoming their own person.
  • We are not entitled to know everything about our adult children.
  • Acknowledging the ways I fell short as a parent does not make me a bad parent. It makes me accountable and willing to grow.
  • Taking mental health seriously is one of the greatest gifts we can give ourselves and our children.
  • Healing our own trauma helps us become healthier parents.
  • Children learn far more from what we model than from what we preach.
  • Admitting my mistakes to my child has been one of the most freeing and healing experiences of my life.

These lessons are not universal truths. They are simply the wisdom I’ve gained through my own experiences. Some came through joy, many through pain, but all have shaped the way I understand relationships, healing, and what it means to love others well.

/2026/07/23/addictive-personality-does-n.title: “Addictive Personality” Does NOT Exist!
/2026/07/23/addictive-personality-does-n.html:
By: Stacy Hixon, MA, LPC-S, CCTP, FRTP

I can’t tell you how many times a day I hear, “I have an addictive personality.” What’s really happening when someone thinks they have an addictive personality? Honestly, it has nothing to do with your personality at all! It’s actually a misunderstanding and malassumption by people who don’t understand psychology.

What is usually happening is some combination of the following:

  • Reward sensitivity: The person may experience stronger reinforcement from substances, gambling, sex, shopping, food, gaming, risk, or attention. The brain learns quickly, “This changes how I feel.”
  • Difficulty tolerating internal distress: The behavior functions as emotional regulation. It may reduce anxiety, numb shame, interrupt boredom, soften loneliness, create excitement, or provide temporary relief from painful thoughts.
  • Impulsivity and reduced pause capacity: The urge reaches behavior before reflective thinking catches up. ADHD, sleep deprivation, trauma, chronic stress, and substance use itself can worsen this.
  • Dopamine seeking: Some people are especially drawn to novelty, intensity, anticipation, and immediate reward. Often the pursuit becomes more reinforcing than the reward itself.
  • Habit learning: Repetition links triggers, urges, and behavior. Eventually, the person may engage almost automatically, even when the behavior is no longer pleasurable.
  • Attachment and regulation difficulties: A person may depend heavily on substances, relationships, work, sex, or other behaviors to feel secure, valued, calm, or connected.
  • Genetic and environmental risk: Family history, early exposure, normalization of substance use, trauma, inconsistent caregiving, and easy access can all increase vulnerability.

What function does the behavior serve, what triggers it, what reinforces it, and what skills or supports are missing?

A person may move from alcohol to gambling, relationships, exercise, shopping, or work because the underlying regulation problem remains unchanged. That is sometimes called addiction transfer, although it is better understood as the same unmet need finding a new delivery system.

So the issue is usually not a defective personality. It is a nervous system and learning system that has discovered a fast, powerful, but costly way to regulate experience.

So, how do we treat it?

We have to treat the function of the behavior, not just remove the behavior.

  1. Identify the pattern

Track what happens before, during, and after the urge.

Ask yourself:

  • What was I feeling?
  • What happened right before this?
  • What did I expect the behavior to do for me?
  • What relief or reward did I get?
  • What did it cost me afterward?
  • This turns “I have no control” into a recognizable cycle.
  1. Name the real need

The urge may be covering boredom, loneliness, shame, anxiety, anger, emotional pain, understimulation, or the need for excitement.

A person cannot replace a behavior effectively until they know what job it was performing.

  1. Build replacement behaviors that match the need

A generic coping skill often fails because it does not provide the same function.

  • For anxiety, use regulation and grounding.
  • For boredom or ADHD understimulation, use novelty, movement, challenge, music, or structured stimulation.
  • For loneliness, use contact and connection.
  • For emotional numbing, use paced emotional processing.
  • For reward seeking, use healthy rewards that are immediate enough to compete with the addictive behavior.
  1. Increase the pause between urge and action

The goal is not to eliminate urges. It is to create enough space for choice.

Helpful strategies include urge surfing, delaying the behavior by ten or twenty minutes, changing locations, calling someone, taking a cold shower, walking, eating, sleeping, or removing access.

Even a brief delay weakens the automatic loop.

  1. Change the environment

Willpower is unreliable when access is easy.

Remove substances, block gambling or shopping apps, avoid high risk settings, reduce cash access, change routines, and create accountability. Environment often matters more than motivation.

  1. Treat underlying conditions

ADHD, depression, anxiety, trauma, sleep problems, chronic stress, and attachment difficulties can all intensify compulsive behavior. Treating those conditions often reduces the need to self regulate through addiction.

  1. Expect substitution risk

A person may stop drinking and begin gambling, dating compulsively, overeating, overspending, or overworking. Recovery should track the underlying pattern, not just the original behavior.

  1. Use structured support

Depending on severity, this may include therapy, group support, medication, substance use treatment, psychiatric care, or medically supervised withdrawal.

For alcohol, benzodiazepines, or heavy substance use, abrupt cessation can be medically dangerous and should be evaluated by a physician.

The person has to move from:

“I need this to change how I feel” to -> “I can experience an urge, regulate myself, and choose what happens next.”

That is less about developing regulation, tolerance, structure, and accountability.
